sources.description: After playing through different fuzzes over the years I discovered that many of them had roots in the same ancestor, the Helios Type 69 Preamp. This preamp spawned such incredible circuits as Roger Mayer’s Octavia Axis Fuzz and even modern releases from dunlop like the Band of Gypsies fuzz. My idea was to go back to make the gain circuit a bit more like the original preamp while also making sure it’s tailored to a guitar’s input. The end design can do anything from clean boosts (when you back off your guitar’s volume control) to heavy distortions and the switchable octave circuit is my nod to the Octavia though the octave section is quite different leading to pretty unique tones due to the fatness of the gain circuit at the heart of the pedal.

Crown browse by type eq/excite/filter/wah wah wah fuzz-wah fuzz wah volume browse by enclosure treadle Crown FW-3 Distortion Wah Volume Published on October 1, 2015 Crown fuzz wah volume foot-controlled treadle Information The Crown FW-3 Distortion Wah Volume is a vintage analog multi-effect pedal produced in the United States by Applied Audio during the late 1960s and early 1970s. Distributed under several brand names including Guild, Atlantic, Kadent, Jax-USA, Lou Rose, Magnum, Nomad, and V-Jay, the Crown version shares identical circuitry with the Applied FW-3 and differs only in branding and minor cosmetic details. It integrates distortion, wah, and volume controls in a single treadle-operated enclosure and is recognized as one of the earliest examples of a multi-function effects pedal. The FW-3 features a robust cast-metal chassis with a steel treadle pedal that operates as both a wah controller and a passive volume pedal when the wah circuit is off. Two rotary controls adjust the output volume and the depth or intensity of the distortion effect. Dual mechanical footswitches independently activate the fuzz and wah sections. The distortion circuit delivers a buzzy, mid-focused fuzz typical of 1960s transistor-based designs, ranging from mild drive to rich, sustaining saturation. The wah circuit produces a broad, vocal sweep with a smooth, moderate resonance, shaped by a ferrite-core toroidal inductor that contributes to the pedal's characteristic warm tone. Internally, the Crown FW-3 uses a fully analog transistor circuit built on a printed circuit board (PCB). This PCB-based layout was standard across nearly all Applied Audio production units, with only a very small number of early Guild examples using handwired point-to-point construction. The circuit typically employs germanium or early silicon transistors depending on production batch, along with carbon-composition resistors and Stackpole potentiometers commonly dated around 1967. The pedal is powered by a single 9V battery (originally type 2U6) and uses mechanical footswitches for true mechanical engagement without buffering. It combines distortion, wah, and volume functions within a single treadle-operated enclosure and was distributed under various brand names including Guild, Crown, Kadent, Jax-USA, Lou Rose, Magnum, Nomad, and V-Jay. The Atlantic-branded version shares its circuitry and layout with the Applied FW-3, differing only in cosmetic presentation. As one of the earliest integrated fuzz-wah designs, it represents Applied Audio's pioneering role in early transistorized effects development. The pedal's construction features a durable cast-metal chassis with a steel treadle and textured rubber grip. The treadle acts as a wah controller when the circuit is engaged and operates as a passive volume pedal when bypassed. Two rotary knobs adjust output volume and distortion intensity, while dual footswitches independently activate the distortion and wah sections. The fuzz circuit produces a buzzy, midrange-forward distortion typical of 1960s transistor designs, with tones ranging from mild drive to thick, sustained fuzz. The wah circuit offers a broad, vocal-like sweep with a flatter resonance than many contemporary designs, shaped by a ferrite-core toroidal inductor that provides a smooth, even tonal response. Internally, the Atlantic FW-3 employs a fully analog transistor circuit mounted on a printed circuit board (PCB). This PCB-based construction was standard across nearly all Applied Audio production units, providing consistency and reliability. Only a limited number of very early examples - mainly Guild-branded units - featured point-to-point wiring. The circuit uses germanium or early silicon transistors depending on production batch, with carbon-composition resistors and Stackpole potentiometers dated to around 1967. sources.description: 136 likes, 15 comments - croytone_audio on October 16, 2024: "After more than a year of preparation, opening a shop in a new country and navigating the challenges of doing all of this in a language I am not very good at, I am extremely excited to announce the release of the first three effects pedals from the new CroyTone Audio Technologies Japan!!!! A ton of work went into these three fuzz pedals and I am extremely proud of the result! The Camper Fuzz, Hae Fuzz and Suzumebachi Fuzz are three distinct flavors of everything I love about fuzz pedals. The Camper Fuzz is the third iteration of my very first circuit I designed back in 2016. Everything I love about vintage style fuzzes in a more consistent and versatile package. From buzzy 60s fuzz tones to loud and heavy 70s sounds, the Camper Fuzz can do it all and more! The Hae is a continuation of an octave fuzz circuit I have been working on for years. Loud, brash and cutting, this fuzz can do all the screaming tones I love about 80s and 90s alternative and shoegaze fuzz. Strong octave and ring mod type tones are available with lots of tonal flexibility and PLENTY of volume. The Suzumebachi Fuzz is a newer design that comes from my love of stacking fuzzes to get a HUGE and thick fuzz tone. Massive doomy wall of sound fuzz tones are available as well as spitting, percussive gated tones. I’m so happy to finally get these out into the world and will begin shipping them out next week. Free shipping on all three pedals in Japan and the US! Available for purchase on my website! And thank you to the amazing @ryejol for designing the artwork on these pedals!".

No one really knows what they look like, some say it’s like a cougar, others say it is a combination of a goat, wolf, and cat. And yet, others say it’s a shaggy giant hyena with red glowing eyes and horns. No matter the physical description it’s horrifying to hear in the wild with it’s long mournful blood-curdling cry. Now you might ask, why Siam Howler and not Ozark Howler? It’s elementary, dear reader. Siam because I went down a rabbit hole of chasing the Siamese Dream tone and found the answer in Thailand. And Thailand is also Siam and Siam is the first four letters in Siamese Dream. So, putting two and two together: The Siam Howler. The Details: I’m a huge fan of The Smashing Pumpkins. Siamese Dream and Melon Collie and the Infinite Sadness were major defining albums in my life. I spent hours (and probably years) listening to them on repeat. We all know The Op Amp Big Muff was a staple on Billy’s board during that time and recently, to me anyway, I was made aware of the MSA Pedal Steel Fuzz that was apparently used as a sweetener on top of the Big Muff. Taking that, I built a MSA Pedal Steel Fuzz, which is basically a Jordon Boss Tone. Then I got the great idea that I should replace all the silicon transistors in it with Russian Germanium transistors. So I did, then I wanted to add different clipping diodes, so I did. Then being me, I decided to take the octave up portion of the Shin Ei Super Fuzz, and put it into this circuit as well. And just because I could, I threw in a voltage starve since nothing says fun like starving Ge transistors of voltage. For those of you who are into mojo parts we have: NOS Russian D9K Ge diodes NOS Russian GT310B transistor NOS Russian MP38B transistor Diffuse yellow LEDs :) Unlike many fuzzes, this one can sit anywhere in the chain and works really well when being stacked after a boost, overdrive, or another fuzz and as a vintage-style low to medium gain fuzz, you might need to boost the signal going into the pedal as some pickups don't provide enough signal. I've found that a Klon-style overdrive or BM-style fuzz can really bring out the rowdy nature of the pedal and add some texture to your tone. Controls: Howl - the volume Hunger - voltage starve to main fuzz circuit Attack - input trim Snarl - tone control Fangs - clipping diode selector (none, yellow LED, Ge - D9K, and Si) Growl - Octave Up tune when it is active Encounter - turn on the effect Shriek - activate octave circuit Power Requirements: 9V DC, negative-tip (Boss-style), not included 10mA current draw when active No batteries (got to keep Mother Earth healthy for the cryptids 👽) Share Share Link Close share Copy link View full details Subscribe to our emails Email Instagram YouTube Payment methods American Express Apple Pay Diners Club Discover Google Pay Mastercard PayPal Shop Pay Visa © 2026, Cryptid Effects Powered by Shopify Privacy policy Terms of service Contact information Choosing a selection results in a full page refresh. Cryptid Effects browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive fuzz browse by type pitch/octave octaver octave fuzz octave fuzz (1 octave up) browse by enclosure pedal Cryptid Effects The Siam Howler Published on April 27, 2026 Cryptid Effects fuzz octave fuzz (1 octave up) pedal Information The Cryptid Effects Siam Howler is a hybrid fuzz pedal that combines multiple vintage circuit influences into a single unit. Its core fuzz circuit is derived from the MSA Pedal Steel Fuzz, itself based on the Jordan Bosstone topology, and is modified through the use of germanium transistors and selectable clipping stages. An additional octave-up section, adapted from the Shin-Ei Super Fuzz, is integrated and can be engaged independently. The design incorporates a voltage-starve control applied to the main fuzz circuit, allowing adjustment of the supply voltage to alter response and gating characteristics. The pedal uses a combination of NOS Russian germanium components, including D9K diodes and GT310B and MP38B transistors, along with selectable clipping options that include no diodes, silicon diodes, germanium diodes, and yellow LEDs. This configuration provides a range of distortion textures from lower-gain vintage-style fuzz to more aggressive, clipped tones. The octave-up circuit includes a dedicated tuning control for adjusting its response when active. The Siam Howler is designed to operate flexibly within a signal chain and can be placed before or after other effects. It responds to input signal strength and may require boosting depending on pickup output, with higher input levels producing more pronounced saturation and harmonic content. It is intended for use both as a standalone fuzz and in combination with other gain stages to shape layered distortion sounds. You will need to be plugged into a quality 9v dc power supply to achieve the best performance and safety of the sensitive germanium transistors in the effect. Effect Signal Flow Your signal starts at the input, IN, and then goes to the Attack control. Attack acts as a signal cut to the rest of the effect. It will not completely mute your signal but it can come very close. In most cases, Attack should be set fully clockwise or backed off from fully clockwise about 10%. From here, it will enter the Sziklai Fuzz circuit which is an interesting two-transistor setup that amplifies the gain of the transistors and seen in many vintage fuzzes (think Spirit in the Sky sounding). Additionally, the germanium transistors provide a more vintage character than is normally seen in this style of fuzz. The Hunger knob controls the voltage being fed to the circuit, the more you raise Hunger , the more gated and sputtery it will become. In general, it is best to set this to fully counter clockwise. Slight application of Hunger can create a mild octave up effect without engaging the Shriek footswitch. If the Shriek footswitch is engaged (LED above the footswitch will be lit), the signal will be routed to a fully analog octave up circuit that will add volume to the signal. This is another vintage-inspired circuit with the ability to tune the octave to your signal by using Growl . Growl will allow you to either add harshness or mellow the octave. It is typically the most pleasant sounding around noon. Growl is interactive with both Attack and Hunger . After leaving the octave up circuitry (or bypassing it completely), we come to a hard clipping stage. Fangs is a 4 position rotary selector. That allows you to add odd order harmonics to the signal. It also can introduce a volume drop depending on the selection. In order of loudest output to softest: None - bypass clipping completely LED - slight signal clipping with symmetrical LEDs Si - stronger signal clipping using symmetrical silicon diodes Ge - strongest signal clippling with Russian D9K diodes (roughly equivalent to 1N34A) Next, the signal will enter the tone control, Snarl . Snarl is a low pass filter that can allow the fully unhinged signal to mellowing it completely by taming the high end treble. Finally, the signal will enter Howl , the volume control. Depending on where The Siam Howler is located on your signal chain and how you've set the other controls, Howl should generally be fully clockwise. From here, the signal leaves the effect via the OUT jack. Internal Trimmers Removing the back cover of the pedal will reveal two to four trimmers (depending on the Siam Howler edition you have). Common to both are octave and mp38a bias and on newer versions, LED brightness trimmers. The LED brightness trimmers are self-explanatory. You shouldn't need to adjust either of these trimmers, but, you can adjust them to your taste. The mp38a bias trimmer adjusts the midpoint of the signal entering the fuzz stage and can introduce more gating into the fuzz. You can't remove it completely as the nature of the fuzz is compressed and gated. The octave bias trimmer allows you to balance the octave up that is heard when Shriek is engaged.
